planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cresthaven needs roughly 800 chill hours to break dormancy properly and performs best in zone 5-8, making it marginal for the mild winters of zone 9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall to size fruit properly. Cresthaven was released by Michigan State University in the 1960s and became one of the standard late-midseason freestone peaches across the Midwest and Northeast, valued for firm, richly flavored, yellow flesh that holds up exceptionally well to canning, freezing, and other preservation, in addition to excellent fresh eating quality. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a peach, tolerating harsher winters than many Southern-bred varieties, but that same trait means it needs a real winter chill to fruit well and is not well suited to the mild winters of the Deep South. Prune annually to an open-vase form for good light penetration and fruit quality, and maintain a regular fungicide and dormant-oil spray program, since brown rot and peach leaf curl affect Cresthaven as they do most peach cultivars.

common_name: Glohaven Peach (Classic Large Commercial Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Glohaven needs roughly 750 chill hours and performs best in zone 5-8, making it marginal in the mild winters of zone 9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall. Glohaven was developed by Michigan State University and became one of the most widely planted commercial freestone peaches in the Midwest and Northeast for decades, prized for very large, firm, attractive fruit with yellow flesh, a red-blushed skin, and a well-balanced, classic peach flavor that holds up well both fresh and processed. The tree is vigorous and reliably productive, with better resistance to bacterial spot than many older varieties of its era, which helped cement its reputation as a dependable commercial standard. Prune to an open-vase form for good light and air circulation, and maintain a regular dormant-oil and fungicide program to manage peach leaf curl and brown rot, common problems across most peach cultivars.

common_name: Suncrest Peach (California Freestone Prized for Exceptional Flavor)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Suncrest has a moderate chill requirement of roughly 500-600 hours, giving it reasonably good adaptability to zone 9 winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Suncrest was bred in California by peach breeder Fred Anderson in the 1950s and became famous, decades later, through farmer-author David 'Mas' Masumoto's writing about the variety's near disappearance from commercial markets despite exceptional flavor, because its relatively short shelf life made it unsuited to long-distance commercial shipping in the era of firm, durable supermarket peaches. The yellow, freestone flesh is richly aromatic, intensely sweet, and complex, widely considered among home orchardists and flavor-focused growers to rank with the best-tasting peaches available, even if it will never win a shipping-durability contest. Grow it as a backyard or local-market tree where fruit can be picked and eaten at full ripeness rather than shipped hard and green, and maintain routine peach leaf curl and brown rot management with dormant-season spraying.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Redskin needs roughly 750 chill hours and is best suited to zone 5-8, marginal for zone 9's mild winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Redskin was released by the USDA in the mid-1940s and went on to become a widely planted mid-20th-century commercial and home orchard peach, valued for firm, yellow, freestone flesh under an attractive skin heavily blushed with red, holding up well to handling and processing while still delivering good, classic peach flavor fresh off the tree. The reliable, productive tree set the standard for decades before being gradually supplanted by newer disease-resistant cultivars, but it remains a solid, dependable choice for home orchards wanting an old-fashioned, well-proven variety. Prune to an open-vase form and follow a routine dormant-season spray program for peach leaf curl and brown rot, which affect Redskin as they do most peach cultivars.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Early Elberta shares its parent variety's roughly 800-hour chill requirement, which accumulates reliably in most zone 9a winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun. Early Elberta is a sport selection of the legendary Elberta peach, the single most historically important commercial peach variety in American horticulture, chosen specifically for ripening one to two weeks ahead of standard Elberta while retaining the same large size, rich yellow freestone flesh, and full, well-balanced classic peach flavor that made the parent variety dominant across the South for a century. The earlier ripening window is a genuine practical advantage for gardeners wanting to beat the peak-summer disease and pest pressure that builds through a long peach season, without giving up the flavor Elberta is famous for. Thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall for good size, prune annually to an open-vase form, and maintain a dormant-season spray program for peach leaf curl and brown rot.
